description: A fast, multi-threaded Redis® and Valkey alternative written in Rust: drop-in compatible, with full-text and vector search built in
license_name: GNU Affero General Public License v3.0
name: kividb
readme_text:
**KiviDB** is a fast, multi-threaded alternative to Redis® and Valkey, written in Rust. It speaks the Redis protocol (RESP2 and RESP3), so existing Redis clients, `redis-cli` and libraries work unchanged, and it has full-text and vector search built in. It runs every core on a sharded in-memory key-value design, and persists to snapshots and an optional append-only file. On the same 32 cores, KiviDB serves **21 million pipelined GETs per second: about 9× Redis 8 and 2.3× Dragonfly**, with under half Dragonfly's p99 latency ([benchmarks](#performance)). ```bash docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb redis-cli -p 6380 PING # PONG ``` KiviDB listens on **6380**, not Redis's 6379, so the two can run side by side; point your client at that port, or pass `--port 6379`. - **Protocol**: Redis-compatible command surface (see [COMMANDS.md](COMMANDS.md) for the supported commands) - **Search and vectors**: Redis Stack–style `FT.*` commands for full-text, tag, numeric and vector (FLAT / HNSW) search - **Lua scripting**: optional Cargo feature. `EVAL`, `SCRIPT`, `FUNCTION`, `FCALL` and related commands are available in builds with `--features lua` (see [Scripting commands (Lua)](COMMANDS.md#scripting-commands-lua)) - **TLS**: optional Cargo feature (`--features tls`) - **Default listen address**: `0.0.0.0:6380`, with [protected mode](#protected-mode) on - **License**: [GNU Affero General Public License v3](LICENSE) (AGPL-3.0-only), open source; using KiviDB does not put your application under the AGPL; see [License](#license) Repository: [github.com/kividbio/kividb](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb) · Website: [kividb.io](https://kividb.io) **Moving from Redis?** [Migration guide](docs/MIGRATING_FROM_REDIS.md) · [Compatibility and differences](docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) · [Client examples](examples/clients/) · [Benchmarks](#performance) · [Releases](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases) · [Kubernetes operator](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb-operator) ### How it compares | | KiviDB | Redis 8 | Valkey 8 | Dragonfly | KeyDB | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | License | AGPL-3.0 | RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPL-3.0 | BSD-3-Clause | BSL 1.1 | BSD-3-Clause | | Language | Rust | C | C | C++ | C++ | | Commands run on | every core (sharded) | one thread (I/O threads) | one thread (I/O threads) | every core (shared-nothing) | several threads | | Full-text and vector search (`FT.*`) | built in | built in (Query Engine) | separate module | built in | no | | Lua scripting | `lua` build | yes | yes | yes | yes | As of October 2026. Something out of date or wrong? Please [open an issue](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues/new/choose). ## Performance *KiviDB 1.2.0 against Garnet, Dragonfly, Redis, Redis Cluster and Valkey. Click for the full-resolution video.* KiviDB 1.2.0 was measured in November 2026 on Azure VMs against Redis 8.10, Redis Cluster, Valkey 9.1, Dragonfly 2.0, Garnet 2.2 and kvrocks 2.17, each on the same machines in the same hour, with p50/p99/p99.9 latency from two load generators. [benchmarks/1.2.0/REPORT.md](benchmarks/1.2.0/REPORT.md) has every number and comparison; [benchmarks/1.2.0](benchmarks/1.2.0/README.md) has the harnesses, raw results and charts. | | KiviDB 1.2.0 | Best other | Redis 8.10 | |---|---|---|---| | `GET` 100 B, pipeline 16 | 10.45M ops/s | Garnet 10.69M | 1.41M | | `SET` 100 B, pipeline 16 | 7.94M ops/s | Garnet 9.83M | 1.25M | | `MSET` of 10 keys | 569K commands/s | Garnet 800K | 144K | | Lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, counters, pipeline 16 | 4.2-6.6M ops/s | Redis Cluster (16 shards): level, ahead on `HSET` and `INCR` | 3.7-6.0x less | | Bytes per key, 100 B values, 50M keys | 140.7 | Dragonfly 141.5 | 174.4 | | Memory added by `BGSAVE`, 30M keys of 1 KB under writes | +10% | Dragonfly +0.4% | +89% | | Filtered vector search, 100 clients | 4,478 q/s | Dragonfly 811 | 1,802 | | Cache hit rate ([#202](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues/202)) | 60.96% | | 60.78% | Where KiviDB loses: Garnet is faster on `SET` at pipeline 16 and on `MSET`; Redis Cluster on `HSET` and `INCR`; Dragonfly uses less memory per vector, during a snapshot, and for ASCII values; Redis ingests vectors faster and serves 3-9% more cache reads a second. These are cloud VMs, so absolute numbers are lower than on the bare-metal machines below.
The charts
### Earlier runs: KiviDB 1.1 on bare metal The figures in this section are from one session in October 2026 on AWS Graviton3 bare metal: the server on a `c7gn.metal` (64 vCPU), confined to 32 cores, and the load generator on a second `c7gn.metal` in the same placement group. Each engine ran alone on the server, one after another. #### Key-value memtier_benchmark through kivi-benchmark's `run-matrix.sh`: 10 million keys, 100-byte values, 30 s a scenario, mean of two rounds; 300 connections pipelined, 1,200 without pipelining. | ops/s | KiviDB 1.1.0 | Dragonfly 2.0.2 | Redis 8.10 | Redis Cluster (32 shards) | |---|------:|------:|------:|------:| | GET, pipeline 16 | **21.2M** | 9.1M | 2.4M | 4.7M | | SET, pipeline 16 | **19.2M** | 8.5M | 2.0M | 4.7M | | GET, no pipelining | 3.07M | **3.35M** | 1.32M | 1.46M | | SET, no pipelining | 3.12M | **3.38M** | 1.54M | 1.46M | | p99 latency, GET / SET, pipeline 16 | **0.36 / 0.42 ms** | 0.88 / 1.07 ms | 2.2 / 2.7 ms | | | Memory per key | 177 B | **134 B** | 178 B | 183 B | #### Vector search [redis/vector-db-benchmark](https://github.com/redis/vector-db-benchmark) on glove-25-angular (1.18M vectors, 25 dimensions): HNSW with M=16 and EF_CONSTRUCTION=256, 100 clients uploading in batches of 64, then queries at ef 64, 128, 256 and 512. | | KiviDB 1.1.0 | Dragonfly 2.0.2 | Redis 8.10 (query engine) | |---|------:|------:|------:| | Queries/s at ef 64 (recall@10) | **59.3k** (0.943) | 41.3k (0.912) | 31.8k (0.912) | | Queries/s at ef 128 | **50.7k** (0.961) | 40.3k (0.937) | 28.9k (0.937) | | Queries/s at ef 256 | 31.5k (0.989) | **36.2k** (0.979) | 21.1k (0.979) | | Queries/s at ef 512 | 18.7k (**0.998**) | **29.8k** (0.995) | 13.7k (0.995) | | Ingest and index build | 31 s | **13 s** | 38 s | | Memory after ingest | 1.66 GB | 1.13 GB | **1.07 GB** | #### Load rising to saturation A second setup, on Azure, in the manner of a latency/throughput/saturation test: rather than one fixed load, clients are added every 30 seconds, 40 to 1,600 per database, until each server can take no more. Each client sends 10 pipelined `SET`+`GET` pairs over 10 million keys, then sleeps 10 ms. Every single server ran on its own 8 vCPU arm64 VM (D8ps_v5); the Redis Cluster had four 2 vCPU VMs, 8 vCPUs in all. KiviDB 1.1.2, October 2026. *The whole run, 20 minutes at 60× speed. Click for the full-resolution video.* | | Peak throughput | p50 / p99 at 1,600 clients | Errors | |---|------:|------:|------:| | KiviDB 1.1.2 | **2.08M req/s** | **4.3 / 13.9 ms** | 0 | | Dragonfly 2.0.2 | 1.56M req/s | 10.1 / 33.9 ms | 0 | | Redis 8.10.2 Cluster (4 × 2 vCPU) | 0.97M req/s | 26.8 / 44.9 ms | 0 | | Redis 8.10.2 | 0.49M req/s | 55.2 / 72.1 ms | 0 | Latency is per pipelined batch. Without pipelining, KiviDB measured about 20% below Dragonfly on these machines (about 8% below on the bare-metal run above). The harness, the run's raw data and its video are in [kivi-benchmark/ramp-saturation](https://github.com/kividbio/kivi-benchmark/tree/main/ramp-saturation); the run's dashboard is a [Grafana snapshot](https://snapshots.raintank.io/dashboard/snapshot/AheJ35tyvNmMmRx3ExXOe2bbsebZIvWg). - Methodology and scripts: [kivi-benchmark](https://github.com/kividbio/kivi-benchmark) - The most recent automated run: [benchmarks/LATEST.md](benchmarks/LATEST.md) Results depend on the environment. Treat published figures as one controlled capture, not a guarantee, and measure on your own hardware and workload. ## Vector search (Redis Stack–style `FT.*`) KiviDB implements **Redis Stack–compatible** search and vector commands, so existing clients and tutorials largely work unchanged. Use them for **full-text (BM25)**, **tags / numerics**, and **vector ANN** (FLAT or **HNSW**) on hash fields. ### Quick start 1. **Create an index** on keys with a prefix, declaring at least one `VECTOR` field (HNSW or FLAT) and optional `TEXT` / `TAG` / `NUMERIC` fields: ```bash redis-cli -p 6380 FT.CREATE idx ON HASH PREFIX 1 doc: SCHEMA \ vec VECTOR HNSW 10 TYPE FLOAT32 DIM 128 DISTANCE_METRIC COSINE M 16 EF_CONSTRUCTION 128 ``` 2. **Store vectors** as raw **FLOAT32** little-endian bytes in a hash field (**`DIM × 4` bytes**), the same convention as Redis Stack and `redis-py` / `numpy` blobs. Use your client's binary-safe `HSET` (the integration tests under `tests/e2e/` have examples). 3. **Query with KNN** (Dialect 2), passing the query vector as a named binary parameter: ```bash redis-cli -p 6380 FT.SEARCH idx '*=>[KNN 10 @vec $q]' PARAMS 2 q DIALECT 2 ``` The full command surface, filters, hybrid search and edge cases are in **[COMMANDS.md](COMMANDS.md)** (search for `FT.CREATE`, `FT.SEARCH`, `FT.HYBRID`, and so on). ### Persistence and restarts - Native snapshots (**`dump.kdb`**) store the **keys**, the **index schemas**, and, when you **`SAVE` / `BGSAVE`** with indexes populated, the **HNSW graph** of each vector field, so search quality after a restart matches the graph you had before shutdown. - While search indexes are being rebuilt at startup, most commands return **`LOADING`** until the rebuild finishes; **`PING`**, **`INFO`** and a few other commands still work. - After a large ingest, run **`SAVE`** (or schedule **`BGSAVE`**) so the next start reloads the graph from disk instead of rebuilding it from the hashes. ## Builds KiviDB comes in four variants, chosen by Cargo features at build time: | Variant | Cargo features | Adds | |---------|----------------|------| | `default` | none | the core server, without Lua or TLS | | `lua` | `lua` | Lua scripting (`EVAL`, `EVALSHA`, `SCRIPT`, `FUNCTION`, `FCALL`, …) | | `tls` | `tls` | TLS listener, and TLS between cluster nodes and replicas | | `full` | `lua,tls` | both | In a build without Lua, the scripting commands return an error. A build without TLS refuses to start if `--tls-port` is given, rather than serving plaintext. ## Building from source Requires a **stable Rust** toolchain ([`rust-toolchain.toml`](rust-toolchain.toml) selects `stable` with `rustfmt` and `clippy`). The crate uses the **2024 edition**; the oldest toolchain it is checked against is **Rust 1.89**, the version the [`Dockerfile`](Dockerfile) builds with. ```bash git clone https://github.com/kividbio/kividb.git cd kividb cargo build --release # default variant cargo build --release --features lua # with Lua scripting cargo build --release --features tls # with TLS cargo build --release --features lua,tls # full ./target/release/kividb ``` On Linux the server uses io_uring when the kernel allows it and falls back to Tokio otherwise (`--io-model auto`, the default). To build the Docker image yourself, `docker build -t kividb .` builds the default variant; `docker build --build-arg KIVIDB_FEATURES=lua,tls -t kividb:full .` builds another one. ## Running KiviDB ```bash ./target/release/kividb # listens on 0.0.0.0:6380 redis-cli -p 6380 PING ``` Any Redis client works; point it at port **6380**. ### Protected mode Protected mode is **on by default**, as in Redis. While it is on, **no bind address has been set** (`--bind` or `bind` in the config file) and the **`default` user has no password**, only clients on the same machine (loopback) may connect. Any other client receives a `-DENIED` error that explains the options, and is disconnected. To accept clients from other machines, do one of these: - set a password: `--requirepass `, or `ACL SETUSER default >`; - set a bind address: `--bind
`; - turn protected mode off: `--protected-mode no`, `protected-mode no` in the config file, or `CONFIG SET protected-mode no` from a local client. If you turn it off or bind to a public address, make sure the server cannot be reached from the internet without a password. ### Linux packages The release page has `.deb` and `.rpm` packages for `amd64` and `arm64`. They install the binary, a systemd unit, a `kividb` system user, and a default `/etc/kividb/kividb.conf` that listens on loopback only. Installing enables and starts the unit, and an upgrade restarts it: ```bash sudo apt install ./kividb_amd64.deb # or: sudo rpm -i kividb.x86_64.rpm redis-cli -p 6380 PING ``` Data (the snapshot, the AOF, `nodes.conf`) lives in `/var/lib/kividb`, and logs go to the journal: `journalctl -u kividb`. To accept clients from other machines, set a password and change `bind` in `/etc/kividb/kividb.conf`. ### Docker Images are published to Docker Hub and the GitHub Container Registry, with the same tags in both: ```bash docker pull kividb/kividb:latest # or docker pull ghcr.io/kividbio/kividb:latest ``` `latest`, `1.2` and version tags such as `v1.2.0` are the default variant; `v1.2.0-lua`, `v1.2.0-tls` and `v1.2.0-full` are the others. Images are built for `amd64` and `arm64`. ```bash docker run -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb ``` A container is reached through its network, never from loopback, so the image's default command is `--protected-mode no`. **Arguments you pass replace that default**, which turns protected mode back on. When you pass your own flags, set a password (recommended) or add `--protected-mode no` yourself: ```bash docker run -p 6380:6380 ghcr.io/kividbio/kividb \ --requirepass "change-me" \ --databases 8 \ --loglevel debug ``` **With AOF persistence** (mount a volume so data survives restarts; the server runs as UID 1000 in `/home/kividb`): ```bash docker run -p 6380:6380 \ -v $(pwd)/data:/home/kividb \ ghcr.io/kividbio/kividb --aof --requirepass "change-me" ``` With `--aof`, every write is appended to `appendonly.aof` and the file is replayed on startup, so a crash loses at most about the last second of writes (the fsync interval) rather than everything since the last snapshot. When an AOF is present it is the source of truth and the snapshot is not loaded; see [docs/PERSISTENCE.md](docs/PERSISTENCE.md) for why. The image is distroless: it has no shell and no `redis-cli`. Connect from another container instead, for example `docker run --rm -it --network container: redis redis-cli -p 6380`. **io_uring in containers:** Docker's default seccomp profile blocks io_uring on recent versions, and KiviDB then falls back to Tokio. To allow it on a Linux host, run with `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (understand what that permits before using it in production). ### Release binaries Release binaries for Linux (x86_64, aarch64) and macOS (Apple silicon, Intel) are published on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases). The `latest/download` links below always resolve to the newest release; replace `latest/download` with `download/v1.2.0` to pin a version. On macOS, Homebrew installs the default variant: `brew install kividbio/tap/kividb`. ```bash # Linux x86_64 curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb-linux-x86_64.tar.gz tar xzf kividb-linux-x86_64.tar.gz ./kividb # Linux aarch64 (an ARMv8.1 CPU or newer: Graviton2 and later, Ampere; not a Raspberry Pi 4) curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb-linux-aarch64.tar.gz # macOS, Apple silicon / Intel curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb-darwin-aarch64.tar.gz curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb-darwin-x86_64.tar.gz ``` Each variant other than the default has its name in the file: `kividb-lua-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `kividb-tls-…`, `kividb-full-…`. The default variant is also packaged for Linux as `kividb_amd64.deb` / `kividb_arm64.deb` and `kividb.x86_64.rpm` / `kividb.aarch64.rpm`, built with [nfpm](https://github.com/goreleaser/nfpm) from [`packaging/nfpm.yaml`](packaging/nfpm.yaml). A `SHA256SUMS.txt` file lists the checksum of every file in a release. ```bash curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb_amd64.deb && sudo dpkg -i kividb_amd64.deb curl -LO https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest/download/kividb.x86_64.rpm && sudo rpm -i kividb.x86_64.rpm ``` From 1.2.0 on, every file in a release and every image carries signed build provenance: a [GitHub artifact attestation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/using-artifact-attestations) that says it was built by this repository's release workflow, from the tagged commit. A checksum proves a download arrived whole; the attestation proves who built it. With the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com): ```bash gh attestation verify kividb-linux-x86_64.tar.gz --repo kividbio/kividb gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/kividbio/kividb:v1.2.0 --repo kividbio/kividb ``` ## Configuration KiviDB is configured with command-line flags, or with a Redis-style configuration file (one directive per line, such as `port 6380` or `appendonly yes`). The file is read from `/etc/kividb/kividb.conf` if it exists; `--configfile ` names another one. A flag given on the command line wins over the same setting in the file. Run `kividb --help` for the full list. | Flag | Default | Description | |------|---------|-------------| | `--port` | `6380` | Port to listen on; `0` for none (TLS only, with `--tls-port`) | | `--bind` | `0.0.0.0` | Address to listen on. Setting it explicitly turns off [protected mode](#protected-mode) | | `--protected-mode ` | `yes` | See [Protected mode](#protected-mode) | | `--threads` | `0` (auto) | Worker threads; auto is the number of cores minus 2 (all cores below 4) | | `--databases` | `16` | Number of databases | | `--dir ` | start directory | Where `dump.kdb`, `appendonly.aof` and `nodes.conf` live | | `--aof` | off | Append-only file persistence | | `--maxmemory ` | `0` (unlimited) | Memory limit | | `--maxmemory-policy` | `noeviction` | What happens at the limit: `noeviction`, or the `allkeys-*` / `volatile-*` eviction policies (`kividb --help` lists them) | | `--loglevel` | `info` | `debug`, `verbose`, `notice` (or `info`), `warning`, `nothing` | | `--logfile ` | standard error | Write the log to a file | | `--log-format ` | `text` | Log line format | | `--io-model` | `auto` | `auto`, `uring` or `tokio` (io_uring is Linux only) | | `--requirepass ` | none | Password for the `default` user | | `--aclfile ` | none | ACL file to load users from | | `--replicaof ` | none | Replicate from a primary | | `--replica-announced-port ` | server port (the TLS port with `--tls-replication yes` or `--port 0`) | Port announced to the primary via `REPLCONF listening-port` | | `--replica-priority ` | `100` | Sentinel promotes the replica of lowest priority first, and never one of `0` | | `--replica-announced ` | `yes` | Whether Sentinel lists this replica | | `--slowlog-log-slower-than ` | off | Slowlog threshold in microseconds (`0` logs every command) | | `--slowlog-max-len ` | `128` | Slowlog entries kept | | `--cluster-enabled ` | `no` | Cluster mode: a cluster bus on ` + 10000`, topology in `nodes.conf`, gossip, failure detection and failover | | `--cluster-node-timeout ` | `15000` | Time without a reply before a peer is suspected to have failed | | `--tls-port ` | `0` (off) | TLS listener (TLS builds only); with `--port 0`, the only one | | `--tls-cert-file`, `--tls-key-file` | none | Server certificate and key (PEM) | | `--tls-ca-cert-file` | none | CA that client certificates are checked against | | `--tls-auth-clients ` | `yes` | Whether clients must present a certificate (only with `--tls-ca-cert-file`) | | `--tls-auth-clients-allowed-names ` | none | Names a client certificate's CN or DNS name must match; `*.` is one label | | `--update-check ` | `yes` | The [startup update check](#startup-update-check) | `maxclients` (default `10000`, in the file or with `CONFIG SET`) counts plaintext and TLS clients, TLS ones from the start of their handshake. At startup KiviDB raises the soft open-file limit to `maxclients` plus what it keeps for itself (32 files, or on io_uring 40 and 8 a worker thread) if the hard limit allows; if not, it lowers `maxclients` to fit and logs a warning. Cluster bus links, a replica's link to its master and files written while saving are not counted in that; leave room for them in a large cluster. ### TLS TLS clients connect on a separate port, `--tls-port`; plain traffic stays on `--port`. With `--port 0` there is no plaintext port, and the server is reached over TLS only (it needs a `--tls-port`; a cluster node needs `--tls-cluster yes` as well, and its bus is then ` + 10000`). A replica of such a master connects with `--tls-replication yes`. ```bash cargo build --release --features tls ./target/release/kividb --port 6380 --tls-port 6381 --tls-cert-file cert.pem --tls-key-file key.pem redis-cli --tls -p 6381 --cacert ca.pem # ca.pem: the CA that signed cert.pem ``` **Client certificates (mutual TLS).** With `--tls-ca-cert-file ca.pem`, clients must present a certificate signed by that CA; others are refused during the handshake. `--tls-auth-clients optional` accepts clients without a certificate but still refuses an invalid one, and `--tls-auth-clients no` does not ask for one. With `redis-cli`: `redis-cli --tls -p 6381 --cacert ca.pem --cert client.pem --key client.key`. **Pinning client certificates by name.** `--tls-auth-clients-allowed-names "*.db1.example admin.example"` (spaces or commas between names) accepts a client certificate only if its subject CN or one of its DNS names matches one of the names; others signed by the same CA fail the handshake, and the server logs the names they carried. `*` stands for exactly one label: `*.db1.example` takes `node-0.db1.example`, not `a.b.db1.example` or `db1.example`. Case does not matter. It applies to clients, replicas and, with `tls-cluster`, nodes on the cluster bus; empty (the default) is off. KiviDB's own setting: Redis has none. **Changed without a restart.** `CONFIG SET` of `tls-cert-file`, `tls-key-file`, `tls-ca-cert-file`, `tls-auth-clients`, `tls-client-cert-file` and `tls-client-key-file` loads the files again for every handshake from then on. `CONFIG SET tls-port ` opens the TLS port (also on a server that started without TLS: `CONFIG SET tls-cert-file cert.pem tls-key-file key.pem tls-port 6381`), moves it, or closes it with `0`; connections already open stay open. `CONFIG SET tls-replication yes` makes a replica's next connection to its master TLS. What cannot be loaded or listened on is refused, and nothing changes. `tls-cluster` needs a restart, and so does `tls-port` on a node with `tls-cluster yes`. **Clients must use TLS on the TLS port.** A plain connection to it (for example `redis-cli -p 6381` without `--tls`) fails the handshake, and the server logs `[TLS] handshake failed`. For memtier_benchmark, add `--tls` (and `--tls-skip-verify` for a self-signed certificate). ### Logs and errors The log goes to standard error, or to `--logfile`. [docs/LOGGING.md](docs/LOGGING.md) describes the log; [docs/ERRORS.md](docs/ERRORS.md) explains the warnings, errors and error replies, and what to do about each. ### Startup update check When it starts, a release build of KiviDB makes **one HTTPS request** to `https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/releases/latest`, the same page you would open to find the newest release. GitHub answers with a redirect to that release's tag; if it is newer than the running build, KiviDB prints a short notice with the link before the startup banner. Nothing is sent but the request itself, with a `User-Agent` of `kividb/`: no host name, configuration, keys, data or identifier. GitHub sees the request's source IP address, as any web server would. Startup waits at most 1.5 seconds for the reply; a failure is logged at debug level only and never affects clients. Only a version-shaped tag is accepted from the reply, and nothing else from it is printed. Any one of these turns it off: - `--update-check no` on the command line; - `update-check no` in the configuration file; - `KIVIDB_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` in the environment. It is also never made by a debug build or when the `CI` environment variable is set. `--update-check-url` points it at another `https://` address, such as a mirror inside a closed network. [docs/UPDATE_CHECK.md](docs/UPDATE_CHECK.md) has the details. ## Contributing Contributions are welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to build, test and submit changes.
